about: Transition families (W2). s1 is the text before the blank; each s2 opens with the blank and relates to s1 by the family's logic. [[...]] marks the two idea spans. fits are the acceptable keys; compatible logics also read correctly and are never offered as wrong; transitions.json also_reads excludes single ambiguous words.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: one species' habit → another species' opposite habit
entries.s1: The female wood frog lays her eggs in [[open ponds]] and never returns to them.
s2: ____, the female Surinam toad [[carries her eggs embedded in the skin of her back]] until they hatch.
____, the male midwife toad [[wraps strings of eggs around his hind legs]] and carries them for weeks.
____, the strawberry poison frog [[comes back to her tadpoles every few days]] to feed them.
____, male glass frogs [[stand guard over their eggs]] on leaves above forest streams.
____, the gray foam-nest tree frog [[lays her eggs in a nest of foam on a branch]] high above the water.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: one hemisphere → the mirror case in the other
entries.s1: In the Northern Hemisphere, the winds of a hurricane [[spin counterclockwise]] around its eye.
s2: ____, in the Southern Hemisphere, the same storms [[spin clockwise]].
____, the cyclones that strike northern Australia [[turn clockwise]] around their eyes.
____, a cyclone forming over the South Indian Ocean [[rotates clockwise]].
____, south of the equator, such storms [[circle in the opposite direction]].
____, cyclones that reach Madagascar [[swirl clockwise]] as they come ashore.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a plant that feeds itself → plants that take food from others
entries.s1: Sunflowers [[make all of their own food]] from sunlight, water and air.
s2: ____, the dodder vine [[draws its food from other plants]] through tiny suckers.
____, the ghost plant [[has no green pigment]] and feeds on fungi in the soil.
____, Rafflesia [[has no leaves at all]] and lives entirely off a host vine.
____, broomrape [[cannot make food]] and attaches itself to the roots of crops.
____, beechdrops [[lack chlorophyll]] and feed on the roots of beech trees.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: water expands as it freezes → other substances shrink
entries.s1: Water [[expands as it freezes]], so ice floats on liquid water.
s2: ____, molten wax [[shrinks as it hardens]], leaving a dip at the center of a candle.
____, most liquids [[grow denser when they freeze]], so their solid form sinks.
____, liquid iron [[contracts as it cools into a solid]].
____, solid carbon dioxide [[sinks]] in its own liquid.
____, frozen olive oil [[settles to the bottom]] of a bottle of liquid oil.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: one heart rate → very different heart rates
entries.s1: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than [[1,200 times a minute]].
s2: ____, a resting human heart [[beats about 70 times]] a minute.
____, an elephant's heart [[beats only about 30 times]] a minute.
____, a blue whale's heart may [[beat as few as 2 times]] a minute during a deep dive.
____, a chicken's heart [[beats around 300 times]] a minute.
____, the heart of a hibernating ground squirrel [[slows to about 5 beats]] a minute.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a feared loss denied → the opposite happened
entries.s1: The marine heat wave [[did not wipe out]] the island's coral colonies.
s2: ____, several colonies [[regained their color]] within a year.
____, most colonies [[survived]] with only minor bleaching.
____, some colonies [[grew faster]] once the water cooled.
____, the colonies [[proved more resilient]] than scientists had predicted.
____, the colonies [[took back their algae]] and began to thrive again.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: one city's government → very different governments
entries.s1: Athens chose its leaders through [[assemblies open to all male citizens]].
s2: ____, Sparta [[was governed by two hereditary kings]] and a small council of elders.
____, Persia [[answered to a single king]] whose word was law.
____, Corinth [[was ruled for generations by one aristocratic clan]].
____, in Egypt [[the pharaoh held power]] as a god on earth.
____, Carthage [[placed power in the hands of wealthy merchant families]].

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: one population count → very different counts
entries.s1: In 1790, the first United States census counted about [[3.9 million people]].
s2: ____, the 1900 census [[counted more than 76 million]].
____, France at that time [[had roughly 28 million residents]].
____, London alone [[held close to a million people]] by 1801.
____, the 2020 census [[recorded over 331 million]].
____, the Qing Empire of China [[numbered around 300 million]] in the same decade.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a plan ruled out → what was done in its place
entries.s1: The delegates who met in Philadelphia in 1787 [[did not simply revise]] the Articles of Confederation.
s2: ____, they [[drafted an entirely new constitution]].
____, they [[set the old document aside]] and designed a new national government.
____, they [[built three separate branches]] of government from scratch.
____, they [[replaced the Articles]] with a framework built around a stronger central government.
____, they [[wrote a plan]] that shifted much power from the states to the nation.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a feared harm denied → the opposite happened
entries.s1: The new railroad [[did not ruin the town]], despite its critics' warnings.
s2: ____, it [[brought the town its most prosperous decade]].
____, the town's population [[doubled]] within ten years of its opening.
____, local farmers [[found new buyers]] in distant cities.
____, it [[turned the town into a busy center]] of regional trade.
____, shops along the main street [[multiplied]] as travelers arrived daily.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: one leader's strategy → rivals' different strategies
entries.s1: Booker T. Washington urged Black Americans to [[focus first on vocational training]] and economic progress.
s2: ____, W. E. B. Du Bois [[demanded full civil and political rights]] without delay.
____, Du Bois argued that a talented few [[should receive a broad university education]].
____, Ida B. Wells [[pressed for immediate public action]] against lynching.
____, the founders of the Niagara Movement [[insisted on equal voting rights]] at once.
____, the NAACP [[went to court]] to challenge segregation laws directly.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: goods flowing one way → goods flowing the other way
entries.s1: Under the colonial trade system, Britain [[exported finished goods]] to its American colonies.
s2: ____, the colonies [[shipped raw materials]] such as timber and tobacco to Britain.
____, the colonies [[sent unprocessed crops]] across the Atlantic to British ports.
____, American ports [[loaded ships with lumber, furs and indigo]] bound for England.
____, colonial planters [[supplied the raw tobacco and rice]] that British merchants resold.
____, the colonies [[were expected to provide raw materials]] and not to manufacture goods of their own.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: one poet's obscurity → contemporaries' fame
entries.s1: Emily Dickinson published [[fewer than a dozen poems]] during her lifetime.
s2: ____, John Greenleaf Whittier [[became a household name]] after publishing Snow-Bound.
____, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow [[saw his books sell in the tens of thousands]].
____, her friend Helen Hunt Jackson [[published widely]] in the leading magazines.
____, Walt Whitman [[paid to print his first book]] and promoted it tirelessly.
____, Elizabeth Barrett Browning [[was celebrated on two continents]] while she was alive.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: admiring description → hostile description
entries.s1: In the novel's first half, the narrator describes the city in [[long, admiring sentences]].
s2: ____, the second half [[reduces the city to short, bitter fragments]].
____, her closing chapters [[describe the same streets with open disgust]].
____, in the final chapters [[she barely mentions the city at all]].
____, after her return from the country, [[her descriptions turn cold and clipped]].
____, the last chapters [[dwell on its noise, dirt and crowds]].

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: what the play does not show → what it shows in its place
entries.s1: The playwright [[does not show the battle]] on stage.
s2: ____, a messenger [[describes it]] in a long speech to the king.
____, the audience [[hears only distant drums]] from behind the set.
____, she [[lets the soldiers' wives imagine it]] as they wait for news.
____, the scene [[stays inside the empty palace]] while the fighting goes on elsewhere.
____, the battle's outcome [[arrives in a single letter]] read aloud in the final act.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: a dismissive reading denied → the opposite reading
entries.s1: Critics at the time [[did not dismiss the novel]] as a mere adventure story.
s2: ____, they [[praised it as a serious study]] of greed.
____, several reviewers [[ranked it among the finest books]] of the decade.
____, one critic [[called it the most important American novel]] since the war.
____, they [[treated it as a work of moral philosophy]].
____, many [[read it as a sharp critique]] of the society that produced it.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: one play's length → much shorter works
entries.s1: Shakespeare's Hamlet runs to [[about 4,000 lines]], making it his longest play.
s2: ____, The Comedy of Errors, his shortest, [[has fewer than 1,800]].
____, Macbeth [[runs to little more than 2,100]].
____, a typical Greek tragedy [[has fewer than 1,600 lines]].
____, The Tempest [[has only about 2,300]].
____, most modern plays [[are well under half that length]].

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a weakness in the study → its results hold anyway
entries.s1: The study [[included only forty patients]], a small number for a clinical trial.
s2: ____, its results [[closely matched]] those of much larger trials.
____, the drop in blood pressure it recorded [[was large enough to matter]].
____, its findings [[are widely cited]] by researchers in the field.
____, the effect it found [[was consistent across every patient group]].
____, the trial [[identified a side effect]] that larger studies had missed.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a warning → the plan goes ahead anyway
entries.s1: The forecast for launch day [[called for heavy storms]] over the site.
s2: ____, the mission team [[kept the launch on schedule]].
____, the engineers [[fueled the rocket]] as planned.
____, the crew [[boarded the capsule]] at dawn.
____, the launch director [[refused to postpone]].
____, thousands of spectators [[gathered along the beach]] to watch.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a strength → a limit the writer grants
entries.s1: The new vaccine [[is remarkably effective]] against the virus.
s2: ____, it [[must be stored at extremely low temperatures]].
____, it [[requires two doses]] given a month apart.
____, [[it is expensive to produce]] in large quantities.
____, its protection [[fades after about a year]].
____, some patients [[run a mild fever]] for a day after receiving it.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a strength → a limit the writer grants
entries.s1: Solar panels [[produce electricity without releasing carbon]] as they operate.
s2: ____, [[manufacturing them]] does release some carbon.
____, they [[generate nothing at night]].
____, their output [[drops sharply on cloudy days]].
____, worn-out panels [[are difficult to recycle]].
____, large solar farms [[take up a great deal of land]].

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: tiny size → remarkable toughness anyway
entries.s1: Tardigrades are [[less than a millimeter long]].
s2: ____, they can [[survive being frozen]] to nearly absolute zero.
____, they [[can endure the vacuum of space]] for days.
____, they [[withstand radiation]] that would kill a human many times over.
____, they [[can survive for years without water]] and revive when it returns.
____, they [[are among the hardiest animals]] ever studied.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: small size → a complex world anyway
entries.s1: Pluto is [[smaller than Earth's Moon]].
s2: ____, it [[has five moons]] of its own.
____, it [[holds a thin atmosphere]] of nitrogen.
____, its surface [[rises into mountains of water ice]] several kilometers high.
____, it [[has a vast plain of frozen nitrogen]] about the size of Texas.
____, it [[may hide an ocean]] of liquid water beneath its crust.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: serious errors → valuable anyway
entries.s1: The expedition's maps of the western territory [[contained serious errors]].
s2: ____, they [[remained the most complete guide]] to the region for a generation.
____, they [[were far more accurate]] than anything published before them.
____, they [[showed the river routes]] more fully than any survey before them.
____, they [[are valued by historians]] as a record of the land before settlement.
____, their account of the rivers [[proved largely correct]].

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a defeat → the campaign goes on anyway
entries.s1: The women's suffrage amendment [[failed in the Senate]] in 1918.
s2: ____, suffragists [[kept pressing]] individual senators for their votes.
____, the movement's leaders [[refused to scale back]] their demands.
____, [[support for the amendment kept growing]] in the states.
____, Alice Paul's pickets [[stayed outside the White House]].
____, activists [[organized new rallies]] in dozens of cities.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a benefit → a cost the writer grants
entries.s1: The Homestead Act of 1862 [[gave millions of acres]] of public land to settlers.
s2: ____, [[much of the best land]] ended up with speculators and railroads.
____, many claims [[were abandoned]] before the five years of required residence were up.
____, the land it offered [[often lay in dry regions]] where 160 acres could not support a farm.
____, [[Native nations lost territory]] as the land was opened to settlement.
____, few formerly enslaved people [[were able to claim]] land under it.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a benefit → a drawback the writer grants
entries.s1: The Erie Canal [[made shipping goods]] from the Great Lakes to New York far cheaper.
s2: ____, [[building it]] required eight years of backbreaking labor.
____, it [[froze solid]] for several months each winter.
____, its narrow locks [[could handle only small boats]].
____, [[within a few decades railroads]] took much of its traffic.
____, the towns it bypassed [[lost business]] to those along its route.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: the wall was breached → it mattered anyway
entries.s1: Invaders from the north [[broke through the Great Wall]] of China several times.
s2: ____, the wall [[slowed most raiders]] enough to give defenders time to gather.
____, it [[helped the empire control trade]] along the frontier.
____, it [[remains one of the greatest building projects]] in history.
____, its watchtowers [[could pass a warning]] hundreds of miles in a single day.
____, the wall [[stood as a powerful symbol]] of imperial strength.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a benefit → a limit the writer grants
entries.s1: The printing press [[made books far cheaper]] in fifteenth-century Europe.
s2: ____, most people [[could not yet read]] them.
____, early printed books [[remained too costly]] for ordinary workers.
____, printers [[often copied errors]] from the manuscripts they worked from.
____, [[church and state authorities]] soon tried to control what was printed.
____, [[scribes who copied books by hand]] lost much of their work.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: early scorn → greatness anyway
entries.s1: Critics dismissed Moby-Dick as [[rambling and strange]] when it appeared in 1851.
s2: ____, it [[is now counted among the greatest]] American novels.
____, a small circle of readers [[admired it deeply]] from the start.
____, [[its opening line]] has become one of the most quoted in literature.
____, its portrait of Ahab [[remains unforgettable]].
____, the book [[is taught in classrooms]] across the country.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: a strength → a weakness the critic grants
entries.s1: The novel's [[portrait of village life]] is vivid and precise.
s2: ____, [[its plot]] moves very slowly.
____, its minor characters [[are thinly drawn]].
____, the ending [[feels rushed]].
____, [[its dialogue]] can be hard for modern readers to follow.
____, the narrator [[rarely explains]] why the villagers act as they do.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: long neglect → a classic anyway
entries.s1: For nearly three decades, Zora Neale Hurston's novel Their Eyes Were Watching God [[was out of print]].
s2: ____, [[its reputation today]] is higher than that of almost any novel of its era.
____, its reputation [[never disappeared entirely]] among writers.
____, it [[is now taught]] in schools across the country.
____, its language [[has influenced generations]] of novelists.
____, it [[is widely regarded as a classic]] of American literature.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: a strength → a weakness the critic grants
entries.s1: The poet's first collection [[shows real technical skill]].
s2: ____, [[much of it imitates]] the poets she admired.
____, [[its subjects]] are conventional.
____, [[few of its poems]] reveal the bold voice of her mature books.
____, it [[relies heavily on rhyme]] that can sound forced.
____, the emotions it describes [[often feel borrowed]].

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: a warning → the author holds firm anyway
entries.s1: The publisher [[warned that the novel's ending would anger readers]].
s2: ____, the author [[refused to change a word]] of it.
____, she [[kept the ending exactly as written]].
____, the book [[went to press]] unchanged.
____, the editor [[printed the final chapter]] as the author had written it.
____, the author [[defended the ending]] in a letter to the publisher.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: feather shape → silent flight and what follows
entries.s1: An owl's flight feathers have [[soft, fringed edges]] that break up the flow of air.
s2: ____, owls [[fly almost silently]].
____, mice [[rarely hear an owl]] until it strikes.
____, owls [[can hear their prey]] over the sound of their own wings.
____, engineers [[have copied the design]] to make quieter fan blades.
____, an owl's approach [[makes far less noise]] than a hawk's.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a heat-trapping atmosphere → extreme surface heat
entries.s1: Venus is wrapped in a [[thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide]] that traps heat.
s2: ____, its surface [[is hotter than Mercury's]], even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
____, [[lead would melt]] on its surface.
____, [[temperatures barely differ]] between its day side and its night side.
____, probes that land there [[survive only an hour or two]].
____, its surface [[stays near 460 degrees Celsius]].

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: acidic soil → what the team did in response
entries.s1: Tests showed that the soil at the restoration site was [[highly acidic]].
s2: ____, the farmers [[planted blueberries]], which thrive in acid soil.
____, the team [[spread crushed limestone]] over the fields to neutralize it.
____, the gardeners [[chose plants that tolerate acid]].
____, the engineers [[coated the new pipes]] to keep them from corroding.
____, the restoration plan [[called for acid-loving native shrubs]].

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: a requirement → what happens if it is not met
entries.s1: The seeds of this plant [[must be kept completely dry]] until planting.
s2: ____, [[they rot]] within weeks.
____, [[mold spreads]] through the whole batch.
____, they [[sprout too early]] and die in storage.
____, [[they lose the ability]] to germinate.
____, [[fungi destroy them]] long before spring.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: water absorbs red light → the ocean's colors
entries.s1: Water [[absorbs red light]] much more strongly than blue light.
s2: ____, the deep ocean [[looks blue]].
____, red fish [[appear gray or black]] at depth.
____, divers' photographs [[lose their reds]] below a few meters.
____, [[many deep-sea animals are red]], a color that makes them nearly invisible.
____, underwater lights [[are usually blue-green]], since that color carries farther.

entries.subject: science
entries.relation: matched spin and orbit → a hidden far side
entries.s1: The Moon [[takes the same time to spin once]] as it takes to orbit Earth.
s2: ____, astronomers [[had to wait for spacecraft]] to map its far side.
____, [[no one had seen the far side]] until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959.
____, [[much of one hemisphere]] can never be seen from Earth.
____, [[radio telescopes on the far side]] would be shielded from Earth's radio noise.
____, [[every photograph of the full Moon]] taken from Earth shows the same markings.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a two-thirds rule → treaties are hard to pass
entries.s1: The Constitution requires [[a two-thirds vote of the Senate]] to approve a treaty.
s2: ____, [[a minority of senators]] can block an agreement.
____, presidents [[often seek support from both parties]] before signing one.
____, some international agreements [[are made as executive agreements]] that skip the Senate.
____, the Treaty of Versailles [[was never ratified]] by the United States.
____, approving a treaty [[is harder]] than passing an ordinary law.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: evidence in a document → what must be true of it
entries.s1: The letter [[describes the Great Chicago Fire]] of October 1871.
s2: ____, it [[cannot have been written]] before that month.
____, the date of 1868 on its envelope [[must be a mistake]].
____, its author [[was alive]] in the autumn of 1871.
____, it [[cannot be the work]] of the merchant who died in 1869.
____, it [[belongs among the papers]] from the 1870s in the collection.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: mountains → how Greek life was shaped
entries.s1: Much of Greece is [[mountainous]], with little flat land for farming.
s2: ____, the ancient Greeks [[built independent city-states]] in separate valleys.
____, many Greek communities [[turned to the sea]] for trade.
____, [[olive trees and grapevines]], which grow on slopes, became key crops.
____, Greek cities [[founded colonies abroad]] when their populations outgrew the land.
____, [[overland travel]] between the cities was slow and difficult.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: early shifts → how the city responded
entries.s1: Surveys showed that most of the city's mill workers [[started their shifts before dawn]].
s2: ____, the transit company [[added early-morning streetcars]].
____, bakeries near the mills [[opened at four in the morning]].
____, the city [[lit the main streets]] through the night.
____, the lunch counters [[began serving breakfast at five]].
____, the union [[held its meetings in the early afternoon]], when the shifts ended.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a requirement → what happens if it is not met
entries.s1: Sailors on long voyages [[needed a steady supply of citrus fruit]].
s2: ____, [[scurvy]] would spread through the crew.
____, [[their gums would bleed]] and old wounds would reopen.
____, many of them [[would grow too weak to work]].
____, [[a long voyage could kill]] half the crew.
____, [[ships would return]] with far fewer men than they set out with.

entries.subject: history
entries.relation: a catastrophic death toll → its effects on labor and land
entries.s1: The Black Death killed [[a third or more]] of Europe's population in the mid-1300s.
s2: ____, [[surviving laborers]] could demand higher wages.
____, [[land fell out of cultivation]] across much of the continent.
____, [[landlords struggled]] to find enough tenants.
____, the old system of serfdom [[weakened in western Europe]].
____, [[many villages were abandoned]] entirely.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: a pigment's date → what must be true of the painting
entries.s1: The white pigment in the painting, [[zinc white]], was not sold to artists until 1834.
s2: ____, the painting [[cannot date from 1820]], as its label claims.
____, the portrait [[must have been finished after 1834]].
____, the attribution to an artist who died in 1830 [[is almost certainly wrong]].
____, the date painted on the frame [[cannot be trusted]].
____, the work [[is younger]] than the museum's catalog suggests.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: serial publication → how the novels were built
entries.s1: Dickens published most of his novels [[in installments]] over many months.
s2: ____, many chapters [[end on a moment of suspense]].
____, his plots [[often sprawl]] across dozens of characters.
____, [[each installment]] had to hold readers' interest on its own.
____, he [[could respond to readers' reactions]] as he wrote.
____, the novels [[run to great length]].

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: an unnamed speaker → how readers respond
entries.s1: The poem [[never names its speaker]] or describes her.
s2: ____, readers [[must build a picture of her]] from what she notices.
____, [[critics disagree]] about who she is meant to be.
____, [[each reader tends to hear]] a different person.
____, the poem [[feels unusually open]] to interpretation.
____, [[some translators]] have given the speaker a name to make the poem clearer.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: a requirement → what happens if it is not met
entries.s1: An actor playing Hamlet [[must pace the soliloquies carefully]].
s2: ____, [[the audience's attention]] drifts during the long speeches.
____, [[the play can run]] well over four hours.
____, [[the character's doubts]] sound like mere hesitation.
____, [[the speeches blur together]].
____, [[the tension of the plot]] slackens.

entries.subject: literature
entries.relation: survey findings → what the museum changed
entries.s1: The museum's visitor surveys showed that [[most people spent less than a minute]] at each painting.
s2: ____, the curators [[shortened the wall labels]].
____, the museum [[hung fewer works]] in each gallery.
____, the staff [[added benches]] in front of the major paintings.
____, the new audio guide [[focuses on a single detail]] in each work.
____, the education team [[began offering slow-looking tours]].
